content: Glomerales is an order of symbiotic fungi that belongs to the phylum Glomeromycota. These fungi are obligate biotrophic mutualists, meaning they rely on a symbiotic relationship with plants for survival. Most members of this order utilize the arbuscular mycorrhizal method, a specialized form of nutrient exchange where the fungi form intricate structures called arbuscules within the root cells of plants to facilitate the transfer of nutrients. These fungi produce large spores, ranging in size from 1 to 5 millimeters. The spores, which include azygospores and chlamydospores, are multinucleate, containing thousands of nuclei within a single spore. Historically, all members of the phylum Glomeromycota were thought to be closely related to the fungal family Endogonaceae. However, molecular sequencing studies have revealed that they are more closely related to the Dikarya, a subkingdom of fungi that includes the Ascomycota and Basidiomycota. The fossil record of Glomerales dates back to the Ordovician period, approximately 460 million years ago, indicating their ancient evolutionary origins. The family name Glomeraceae, which serves as the basis for the order name Glomerales, was historically misspelled as Glomaceae, leading to the incorrect spelling of the order as Glomales. These errors are correctable under the rules of the International Code of Botanical Nomenclature. Despite this, the incorrect spellings are still frequently encountered in scientific literature.
